analysis.one_liner: Creates a free one-stop FTC system to delete your personal data from all data brokers at once.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote, despite being introduced by a Republican senator with Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company that buys and sells people's personal data (a "data broker") to register with the Federal Trade Commission and disclose what it collects. The FTC would then build a single public website where anyone could, with one free request, order every registered data broker to delete their information and stop collecting it. Data brokers would have had to delete matching records within 31 days, submit to outside audits every three years, and pay fees to fund the system.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who wants their personal information removed from the data-broker market — which today means submitting separate, often hard-to-find opt-out requests to each company. The bill was aimed especially at people at risk of stalking, harassment, identity theft, and scams, since brokers sell location and contact data to anyone willing to pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose data is sold by brokers

how_it_helps.text: One free request through an FTC website would reach every registered data broker, instead of individuals having to track down dozens of companies one by one.
Data brokers and their affiliates would have had to delete matching records and stop future collection within 31 days of a match, and confirm to the FTC how many records they deleted.
Brokers would have to register annually and disclose what data they collect and where they get it, with the list published in a machine-readable public format.
Every data broker would face an independent third-party audit of compliance every three years, with reports kept on file for six years and submitted to the FTC.
The FTC could enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, backed by its existing penalty powers.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, who would lose the ability to keep selling information about people who opt out, and would bear registration, deletion, audit, and system-funding costs. Some cost falls on advertisers and other businesses that rely on broker data, in the form of smaller or less rich datasets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and the ad-data trade

drawbacks.text: The centralized system would collect email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, and other identifiers in hashed registries run by the government, creating a high-value target; the bill requires security safeguards but a breach would be catastrophic.

The bill excludes several large categories of data holders, including credit reporting agencies, fraud-prevention and identity-verification services, and news organizations, so data held by those firms would not be covered.
Enforcement depends on brokers self-reporting deletion counts to the FTC and on the agency's willingness and capacity to police the system through rulemaking and cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For individuals, the benefits are real and direct: a free, single way to escape a market that most people cannot navigate manually, where the same data is used for identity theft, stalking, and scam targeting. The main risks are the security of the government's own registry and the long list of excluded companies that would remain outside the system. The core trade — a small attack surface at the FTC versus an unmanageable status quo for individuals — weighs on the side of the bill, though the exclusions blunt its reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the DELETE Act on June 22, 2023, with Sen. Jon Ossoff, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill after introduction, giving it bipartisan support.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers are better off: without a law, there is still no single government-run deletion request they are required to honor, and the market for buying and selling personal information continues unchanged. The FTC was also spared the cost and risk of building and securing the centralized system.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, whose market stays untouched

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DELETE Act and sent it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. Jon Ossoff
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

for.name: Two Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 22, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Data broker industry
against.what_they_did: Companies in the data-broker market publicly opposed mandatory registration and centralized deletion requirements during consideration of the bill and its House companion.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill with a Democratic original cosponsor and two more Democratic cosponsors; the bill was never opposed on any recorded vote because it never reached one.

industries.note: These companies make money selling personal information about people who never dealt with them directly. The bill would force deletion of opted-out individuals' records and stop future collection, cutting off that revenue; that loss is the public's gain.

industries.industry: Digital advertising and marketing data ecosystem
industries.note: Advertisers and analytics firms buy from brokers, so mass deletion requests would shrink available targeting data. Some users would also lose a form of free, ad-supported content that is funded by this data.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and fraud-prevention/identity-verification firms
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes credit reporting agencies and fraud/identity-verification companies from its definition of data broker, leaving their existing legal frameworks and business roles untouched even as brokers generally are regulated.
